newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan wages to rise, but no boost for economy.
newsitem.headline: Japan wages to rise, but no boost for economy.

text.p: Japan's major firms on Tuesday offered higher wage hikes for the next business year, but analysts said the rise is too small to power personal consumption or boost the overall economy.

Management in the key car, electronics, shipping and steel industries offered an average wage hike of around three percent or below for the year starting in April, compared with an actual 2.86 percent, or 8,712 yen ($70) per month, rise in 1996/97.

The latest wage hike offer, in response to requests from unions belonging to the Japan Council of Metal Workers' Unions, will have a big influence on other industries in the "shunto", or spring offensive, wage talks.

The planned increase in wages was in line with recovering corporate profits, aided by the weak yen which raised export incomes. But the wage hikes varied, depending on each firm's business performance.
But the wage hike is expected to do little to prompt cash-strapped Japanese consumers, facing a hike in the national sales tax in April, to loosen their purse strings.

"The wage hike appears slightly larger than the previous year's hike," said Nobuyuki Saji, a senior economist at Nikko Research Centre. "But it would be too small to offset the likely damage on consumption from the planned sales tax hike."
A top business leader on Tuesday echoed that view, saying the wage increase will not push up overall economic growth.
"I cannot say that the wage hike would immediately affect consumer confidence," Jiro Nemoto, chairman of the Japan Federation of Employers' Association, told a news conference.
"Given the planned sales tax hike, I don't think the wage hike will push up gross national product," he added.
Japan is due to raise the sales tax rate to five percent from the current three percent on April 1, adding a tax burden of about 5 trillion yen ($40.6 billion) to the Japanese public.
Saji also said smaller companies, responsible for the majority of Japan's overall work force, may face difficulties in raising wages by a similar margin as their larger rivals.
Japan's top carmaker Toyota Motor Corp said it has agreed to a monthly wage increase of 9,400 yen ($76), or 2.83 percent, compared with last year's hike of 8,700 yen ($70).
Toyota also said it accepted the union's request to pay bonuses equal to 6.1 months' of basic wages, or an average of 2.08 million yen ($16,900), compared to 5.8 months last year.
Nissan Motor Co Ltd, the nation's second-ranked carmaker, said it had agreed to a monthly wage hike of 9,000 yen ($73), up from last year's 8,300 yen ($67) increase.

Japan's top 17 electronics makers have agreed on a monthly rise of an average 9,027 yen ($73), a rise of 200 yen ($1.50) over last year's rise, the second straight year the rise has exceeded the previous year's.

Telecom giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT), also said it had agreed with its unions on a monthly wage hike of 9,900 yen ($80) or 2.86 percent, up marginally from the previous year's 2.8 percent rise.
It is the first time the increase has been bigger than the previous year's since 1990.
Under a system introduced 40 years ago, management and labour representatives engage in "shunto" talks in February and March to seek unified wage hikes through collective talks.

This year, labour called for higher wages due to the tax hike, but management went into negotiations cautiously, given stable domestic prices and competition from lower-wage workers from other Asian nations. ($1=123 yen)
